newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Italy isolated in Club Med race for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Italy isolated in Club Med race for EMU.

text.p: Spain and Portugal stole a march on Italy in a race among the European Union's southern members to join a single currency, after the European Commission on Monday gave Rome a stern warning on its public finances.

Sharp differences in assessing the progress of the so-called Club Med countries to rein in expenditure ahead of the single currency, expected in 1999, emerged at a meeting of EU finance ministers to review the 15-nation bloc's budgetary situation.
For Italy, the news was far from encouraging.

A Commission report, used by the ministers in the EU's so-called excessive deficits procedure, said Italy's control of pubic spending in 1996 had been "insufficient", with more needed to ensure lasting budgetary consolidation.
With regard to its 1997 budget plan, the EU executive urged Rome to replace one-off savings items with structural measures which would have a "permanent impact on the budget".
The EU executive also called on Italy to bring its 1998 budget deficit below three percent of Gross Domestic Product.
One EU diplomat called the report "sharply pointed" but Italian officials reactly calmly, stressing the achievements Italy has made in curbing spending over the last few years.

Italy's Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told reporters in Brussels that the Commission recognised Italy was making a "tremendous effort" and said relations between Brussels and Rome were of an "extreme clarity."
In April, the Commission incensed Rome when it forecast Italy's 1997 budget deficit at 3.2 percent of GDP, just above the Maastricht treaty's three percent target.
But, for Spain and Portugal -- which have tried hard to distance themselves from Italy in terms of public perception -- the Commission's evaluation was glowing.
Both governments presented updated economic convergence plans designed to map out how they plan to bring public deficits in line with Maastricht ahead of 1999.

For Portugal, seen by many analysts as best placed among the southern bloc for timely entry to EMU, the EU "noted with satisfaction the progress made by Portugal in bringing down inflation and reducing budgetary imbalances."
In addition, the EU said the "economic assumptions underlying (Portugal's) programme were considered realistic."
Much the same was said for Spain.
The group praised a two-pronged strategy that promotes economic growth and employment on a permanent basis "through budgetary consolidation and structural reform."
A key element in both evaluations was the emphasis on structural budgetary reform, something absent from the review of Italy's recent performance.
EU officials have repeatedly stressed the importance of durable and sustainable budgetary consolidation in assessing which countries would qualify for EMU in 1999.

In Italy's case, the absence of such reforms may be its biggest hurdle in joining on EMU on time, with projections for its 1998 budget deficit seen rising due to the heavy reliance on one-off savings this year.
Italy's Ciampi, recognising the need for further budgetary savings, said the government's 1998 budget deficit would in fact fall below three percent of GDP.
A decision on those countries joining the first wave of monetary union is expected to be taken next spring.
